The best place to start would be an app called "Headspace". The app gives you 10 sessions (1 per day) for free.

Also, I always found this post helpful on reddit:

Mindfulness of breathing:

A) Focus on the breath. Pick either a physical sensations (e.g: the rise and fall of the abdomen, the breath passing through the nose, the breath passing the tip of the nose, etc... ), a mental concept ("in" and "out", or a point in space that the breath passes, or the process of the rising and falling of the abdomen, etc... ) or both.

B. The mind will begin to wander. When you notice it has (a moment of mindfulness) return focus to the breath.

C. Rinse and repeat.

^ That right there is essentially what meditation is.

Honestly, I don't think most Android tablets are very good for reading. I've owned a Asus Transformer TF101, HP Touchpad, Surface Pro, Dell Venue Pro (the 7" Windows one), and now iPad Air 2 and my observations are:

  • 16:9 sucks for reading. Too wide for landscape reading and too narrow for portrait. The aspect ratio might be good for watching videos, but that's only really because most content is in 16:9 or wider. I haven't found 16:9 to be very comfortable to hold at around 9-10". Stick to 4:3 if you really want to be reading on it
  • I find 7" to be small, but a lot of people are fans of the Nexus 7. The iPad Air at 9.7" is really the maximum I feel comfortable with and I think I would like an 8" screen even better.
  • The size/weight/thickness of the device matters, a lot. I love my Surface Pro but I never really use it as a tablet because the damn thing is so thick and large. The HP Touchpad was definitely more fatiguing to my hands because it was thicker, heavier, and had much larger bezels than my iPad Air 2.
  • Although most tablets these days have fairly good ppi, don't cheap out and get something with low screen resolution or quality. You will notice how much nicer it is to read on a good screen.

Tablets are really hard to be completely satisfied especially since they come at so many more sizes, shapes, and price ranges than phones. Specs (RAM, CPU, battery, screen) can be all over the place with tablets too, since most manufacturers use smaller tablets are a way of cheaping out on the components so you end up with mid-range 7-9" tablets and flagship 10.1" tablets. Honestly, I wouldn't feel comfortable using a budget tablet. The Galaxy Tab S 8.4 at $300 is probably the cheapest Android I would go with, but it's hard to make a case for that when the iPad Mini 2 is $300 new and is 4:3 rather than 16:9. At $400 there are a lot of good options out there like the Nexus 9, Dell Venue 8 7000 (who comes up with the names?), Fire HDX 8.9, and iPad Air (1st generation).

Oh and if you want good screen-on-time on Android, definitely try rooting and Greenify aggressively. The iPad gets awesome battery life, but iOS is a lot more aggressive about background apps than Android is.
